Rock volume estimation from incomplete point clouds using interpretable
machine learning for rockfill material gradation analysis
Jiayu Wang a,1, Mengnan Shi a,1, Yilong Wu b, Peng Ji a, Hongtao Li a, Qiang Yao a,c,*
a State Key Laboratory of Hydraulics and Mountain River Engineering, College of Water Resource and Hydropower, Sichuan University, Chengdu, Sichuan 610065, China
b Sinohydro Bureau 7 Co., Ltd, Chengdu, Sichuan 610213, China
c Technology Innovation Center for Risk Prevention and Mitigation of Geohazard, Ministry of Natural Resources, Chengdu, Sichuan 611734, China


H I G H L I G H T S                   G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T

• Proposed  a  rock  volume  prediction
 method using 2.5D point clouds and
  interpretable machine learning.
• Achieved high accuracy with R2 = 0.979
 and MAPE = 9.39% using a LightGBM
  model.
• SHAP analysis revealed particle volume
 and  surface  area  as  key  predictive
  features.
• Automated gradation detection work­
  flow showed less than 2% error across
  all size ranges.





A R T I C L E  I N F O                  A B S T R A C T

Keywords:                                       Accurate particle size distribution and volume estimation are fundamental to understanding the behavior of
Particle size distribution                            granular materials like rockfill in geotechnical applications. However, conventional sieving is labor-intensive,
2.5D point clouds                             and 2D imaging methods fail to capture true 3D morphology, introducing systematic bias in volume predic­Machine learning framework                                                        tion. While 3D laser scanning offers richer geometric data, real-world scans yield only partial (“2.5D”) pointVolume prediction                                                clouds due to occlusion, severely limiting direct volume calculation. To address this, we propose an interpretableGradation analysis
                                           machine learning framework for estimating complete particle volumes from incomplete 2.5D point clouds,
                                                enabling high-accuracy gradation analysis. A dataset of 400 paired 2.5D and complete 3D particles was con­
                                                    structed from real rockfill materials. Morphological analysis revealed consistent shape distributions across sizes,
                                                supporting a generalized model. Using LightGBM, we developed a volume prediction model solely from 2.5D-
                                                derived 3D features, achieving exceptional accuracy (R2 = 0.979, MAPE = 9.39%). SHAP analysis provided
                                                  physical interpretability, identifying particle volume and surface area as dominant predictors. Integrated into a
                                                              full pipeline — including segmentation and size classification — the automated workflow was validated on six
                                                   synthetic stockpile cases generated from realistic morphological distributions, yielding gradation errors less than
                                2% across all size fractions, with predicted curves closely matching ground truth.

2. Methodology

   In research on gradation detection of rockfill materials based on 3D
point clouds, point cloud segmentation methods extract rock particle
point clouds from stockpile scans to calculate particle size and volume.
The volumetric proportion of particles within different size ranges is
then  statistically determined to achieve gradation calculation and
analysis. However, current 3D laser scanning technology can only cap­
ture the upper morphology of particles (“2.5D particles”), failing to
penetrate and capture lower surfaces. Consequently, the segmented rock
particles retain only partial surface point clouds, leading to significant
errors when  calculating  volumes  using  mainstream  convex  hull
methods, thereby increasing gradation detection inaccuracies.                            Fig. 1. Computation of principal particle dimensions.
